lines.text: III
Just as none of us, even those who are most disappointed,
should look back without gratitude, so none should fail to
ask himself the searching question, "Where have I failed?
what has remained undone?" And if he faces the test of this
inner self-examination, if he discovers where he has been
neglectful, and what should be improved in the future-and
which of us must needs not confess so much?—is it really
enough to make up one's mind to do better in the future?
There is no doubt that at the end of next term we shall again
have to look back in shame on the things we have failed to
do and the points at which there is room for improvement,
and so on throughout the entire course of our lives. We
should have to have a great deal of time at our disposal if
we were really to make up for what we have neglected, and
the truth is that we have no such extra time to dispose of.
Each future to which we look forward brings its own tasks,
and what is gone, is gone for ever. Our lives are inescapably
caught up in the ever-flowing time stream. Who knows how
soon he will have used up this available time? We do not lay
hold of peace by our repentance and good intentions; we
remain in perpetual dispeace and restlessness.
This state of affairs suggests that our repentance has not
the power to make us better. We always remain the same;
we are not masters of ourselves. If it is the case that a retro-
spective glance such as we are taking to-day always shows
that our consciousness includes the twofold feeling-grateful
joy and tormenting shame-then this is no incidental thing
but rather is suggestive of the very pattern and structure of
our being. This characteristic is the fissure that runs through
it. The really torturing and painful thing is not the particular
actions in which we have erred or which we have failed to
perform, but just this: the inescapable dualism in our nature.
"Dein Psalmist, mein Vater, hat wider seine Feinde gesungen,
Und ich, mein Vater, folge ihm, und singe einen Psalm hier
wider meinen Feind!
